newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore PM says slandered by opposition leader.
newsitem.headline: Singapore PM says slandered by opposition leader.

text.p: Singapore's leaders went to the court again on Monday to accuse an opposition figure of defamation in a case being monitored by international rights bodies.

Joshua Jeyaretnam was committing defamation by innuendo when he told an election rally that a colleague had filed police complaints against Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and other senior figures accusing them of lying, Goh's lawyer said.

Tom Shields told the packed High Court that Jeyaretnam, speaking on the eve of January 2 elections in which Goh's People's Action Party (PAP) won 81 of parliament's 83 seats, knew the complaints were unfounded.
"This is a classic innuendo situation," said Shields, a top London lawyer. Goh's case opened a scheduled 12-day hearing into 11 defamation suits against Jeyaretnam.
The 71-year-old Workers' Party leader, a veteran of courtroom battles against PAP leaders, said he would fight the case "all the way".
Lee Kuan Yew, Goh's predecessor, and nine other PAP leaders are also suing Jeyaretnam in the case, which is being monitored by international human rights bodies.

"Amnesty International is concerned at reports that the Government of Singapore has used civil defamation suits against political opponents in a manner that violates their right to freely hold and peacefully express their convictions," the London-based organisation said in a statement.
The PAP leadership denies using the courts to silence the opposition. It is a question, Goh has said, of challenging allegations that would undermine his ability to govern.

The case against Jeyaretnam is the second this year against a Workers' Party member. As in the earlier trial, the allegations stem from the election campaign when the PAP turned all its weapons on Tang Liang Hong of the Workers' Party.
They accused Tang of being "an anti-Christian, Chinese chauvinist" who endangered racial harmony in predominantly ethnic Chinese Singapore, which has substantial minorities of Malays and Tamils.
Tang filed complaints to the police charging Goh and his colleagues with lying. They sued him for libel and Tang fled Singapore saying his life had been threatened.

He did not return to defend himself and the cases were awarded to the PAP leaders. They won a record S$8.08 million (US$5.65 million) in damages and then sued Jeyaretnam, accusing him of endorsing Tang's charge of lying.
"Mr Tang Liang Hong has just placed before me two reports he has made to police against, you know, Mr Goh Chok Tong and his people," Jeyaretnam told the election rally.
Shields said that amounted to an endorsement of Tang's charges against Goh, which had been widely publicised. No one in Singapore could have been unaware of them, he said.
"In the context of that evening, the message is clear," Shields said.
"It was being presented that the plaintiff (Goh) and his people had done something seriously wrong. The defendant was standing shoulder to shoulder with Mr Tang."
Shields said Jeyaretnam had offered an apology to Goh and the other PAP leaders after the incident but it was inadequate because it had not stated that Tang's claims were baseless.
Over the years, Jeyaretnam has paid damages of more than S$780,000 to former prime minister Lee, his main PAP courtroom opponent.
In the most famous of Jeyaretnam's legal battles, he and a co-defendant were jailed for a month and fined S$5,000 in 1986 for making false statement over Workers' Party accounts.

He appealed to London's Privy Council, the highest court for many Commonwealth nations. It said Jeyaretnam and his co-defendant had been "publicly disgraced for offences of which they were not guilty", although the finding was only advisory.
Singapore later abolished appeals to the Privy Council.
